The whole point of TypeScript, for me, was supposed to be that the type system catches mistakes before they become runtime bugs. So when AI got reliably good at generating precise, well-structured types from a description or an existing shape of data, I stopped thinking about types carefully myself and just asked for them whenever I needed one. Six months of this. Our codebase had genuinely excellent type coverage by any measure you’d want to check.
Then a production bug traced back to a type that was, technically, completely accurate and completely useless for catching the actual problem, because the type described the shape of the data correctly while the actual bug was about a business rule the shape alone could never express.
Why the type coverage felt like real safety
Every interface, every generated type, matched the actual data shape being used, precisely, with no loose any types hiding anywhere, exactly the discipline TypeScript is supposed to reward. Autocomplete worked beautifully everywhere. Refactors that touched shared types threw compile errors in exactly the right places when a shape changed. This is, genuinely, most of what people mean when they say TypeScript is paying off, and for…
